VTOL Drone Burns Jet Fuel to Charge Batteries and Fly for 1,300 Miles
6 photos
Photo: Skyways
There are so many new and relatively new companies in the business of making drones in one form or another that it is almost impossible to keep track of them all. Luckily, from time to time, some of these businesses come into the spotlight with something fresh, exciting, or otherwise remarkable. Like, say, a new vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) cargo aircraft that will commence operations by the end of the year.
The crew behind this design is Texas -based Skyways, a company that has been around for about a decade or so to develop autonomous aviation solutions. It has tried to do so with something called the V2, but that's not what we're here to discuss. That would be something called the Skyreach.
Presented this week as a long-range Group 3 autonomous VTOL meant to carry cargo, the aircraft is getting ready to enter service in the hands of undisclosed defense and commercial customers as soon as next month.
The drone has a lot of things going for it, as most other drones do, but it is one capability that stands out the most: range. That would be a highly impressive 1,300 miles (2,092 km) of travel one way and a total flight time of 18 hours, with some footnotes.
The Skyreach can fly that far thanks to the dual hybrid system that powers it. It combines a series of batteries to power its eight electric motors, and a heavy-fuel engine (which can burn JP-5 and Jet A-1 fuels) that is used, aside from cruising, to recharge the batteries in flight. This eliminates the need to recharge or swap batteries.
The hybrid system can get the drone to its maximum distance when carrying only ten pounds (4.5 kg) of stuff and the maximum fuel load – the thing can only fly while carrying 100 pounds (45 kg) of combined fuel and payload – and, naturally, that drops when more weight is added.
Another thing that makes the design special is the configurable payload bay, which can be specced so that cargo of different shapes, sizes, and uses, including temperature-controlled items, can be loaded and transported. Then, the design can fly in winds as powerful as 40 knots and in temperatures ranging from minus 5 degrees Fahrenheit to 120 degrees (minus 20 degrees Celsius to 49 degrees).
Skyways said the drone can be flown at a high frequency, and as most other VTOLs out there, it does not need runways to take off and land. On top of that, we're also told it costs one-tenth the price of a helicopter, but, to be fair, helicopters are a lot more capable than this.
As said, the Skyreach is expected to fly operationally as soon as December 2026. It's unclear how many of them are in the hands of customers, but Skyways revealed that it plans to have some 1,000 of them in the skies over the next five years, serving both commercial and defense needs.
